timecoded_text_to_speech.text: Music
Martin, you founded your own film festival in North-Hermes, Faelia.
How did you start with that idea when it had come up?
At first it wasn't a festival proper.
It was a monthly film series which I started because there wasn't anything queer in cinemas in our area.
So I started with that and it grew from one city to six cities and after a time another festival in Cologne more or less died.
And I took heritage of that. I founded a new festival to fill the gap and have more LGBT cinema in my area.
So LGBT topics are becoming rare in Syria where you live?
It's not that it became rare but it's more or less it is rare except for the big films, the Danish girl or Pedro Almotovar films.
It's rare that films with LGBT content get into cinemas anywhere in Germany.
Although it's a metropolitan area, it's not much of an issue in cinemas except for the big names because they sell and the smaller films they don't really sell.
So the cinemas don't focus on them.
So this is your principle, your idea with this festival that you just show smaller films like smaller productions.
What usually wouldn't be screened in a cinema?
I wouldn't mind showing the big productions if we got them.
But sometimes it's difficult because the distributors in Germany if they have a big name to a film, they have their own agenda to putting the film into festivals or into cinemas.
And they don't really care much about the smaller festivals.
So if we got those bigger films, I wouldn't mind that.
But it's just that I want to have LGBT cinema at all.
Otherwise there wouldn't be anything except for the big productions.
But there are so many topics which the big productions don't cover or don't cover in the queer native aspects that smaller productions might have.
Or they are not so deep in the topic.
If it's like for a special queer or LGBT community, it's dealing different with the subject.
What do you mean?
Now you are a jury member. So you switch from an organizer to a jury member. How is that feel?
Well, the last couple of years I've been here as a press because I write for a gay magazine.
So I'm already used to Berlinale in a way.
But being a jury member you have different duties. It's organized in a different way.
It's very interesting to meet all the international colleagues who have their own stories and their own views.
It's different. It's exciting. It's new.
So you're having fun with the other jury member?
I like them very much. They are fun. They are so interesting and so intelligent and so nice.
I hope we grow together in the next couple of days.
You have a few days left.
Oh, we're just starting.
I see. So something what fascinates you the most or what's fascinating for you about film?
So why is film so important for you?
For me it was always a way to connect with emotions, to feel something.
And that's what I find most important about movies that they touch me.
And if they touch me then it's a good movie.
Of course I also appreciate beautiful cinematography and good acting.
Of course with a good acting comes the feeling.
But I appreciate technicality but I most appreciate feelings about stories, about what filmmakers or the actors try to portray or convey.
So we're already done. I wish you good films and the screenings.
Thank you.
A lot of fun and see you at the Teddy ceremony.
Thanks Martin.

youtube_description: Martin Wolkner studied Linguistics and Film Studies and is the founder and head of homochrom. Established in 2009 as a monthly film series in six cities in North-Rhine Westphalia, homochrom was expanded by a queer film festival in Cologne and Dortmund in 2011. Wolkner initiated the debut film award and federal funding of the German festival co-operation QueerScope in 2016. As a member of the German Film Critics Association he writes for the gay magazine Box, among others. Martin Wolkner has previously worked for the International Women’s Film Festival Dortmund | Cologne and is working in subtitling. Currently he is developing his own film projects as a writer.
